messages.content: What is the difference between a hot site, warm site, and cold site in disaster recovery?

These are three levels of disaster recovery facilities. A hot site is a fully operational duplicate of your primary data center — it has all hardware, software, data (replicated in real-time), and network connectivity ready to go. Failover can happen within minutes to hours. Most expensive but provides the lowest Recovery Time Objective (RTO). A warm site has hardware and network infrastructure in place but may not have the most current data — it requires restoring from recent backups and some configuration before going live. Failover typically takes hours to a day. Moderate cost. A cold site is essentially empty space with power, cooling, and basic connectivity — no hardware or data pre-installed. In a disaster, you'd need to procure and set up hardware, install software, and restore data from backups. Recovery can take days to weeks. Least expensive for ongoing costs. The choice depends on your RPO (Recovery Point Objective — how much data loss is acceptable) and RTO (Recovery Time Objective — how quickly you need to be back online), balanced against budget. Many organizations use a tiered approach: hot site for critical systems, warm site for important systems, and cold site or cloud-based DR for non-critical workloads.
How do you configure SNMP monitoring on a network switch?

SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) enables centralized monitoring of network devices. Configuration steps for a managed switch: 1) Access the switch CLI via console cable or SSH. 2) Enable SNMP and configure community strings (SNMP v1/v2c) or users (SNMP v3). For Cisco switches: 'snmp-server community publicRO RO' (read-only) and 'snmp-server community privateRW RW' (read-write). Change these from defaults! For SNMP v3 (recommended — encrypted and authenticated): 'snmp-server group MonitorGroup v3 priv', 'snmp-server user MonitorUser MonitorGroup v3 auth sha AuthPass123 priv aes 128 PrivPass123'. 3) Configure SNMP traps to send alerts to your monitoring server: 'snmp-server host 10.0.1.50 version 2c publicRO' or for v3: 'snmp-server host 10.0.1.50 version 3 priv MonitorUser'. 4) Enable specific trap types: 'snmp-server enable traps snmp linkdown linkup coldstart', 'snmp-server enable traps config', 'snmp-server enable traps cpu threshold'. 5) Set the system contact and location: 'snmp-server contact admin@company.com', 'snmp-server location ServerRoom-Rack4'. 6) On your monitoring platform (PRTG, Nagios, Zabbix, LibreNMS), add the switch as a device with the matching SNMP credentials. Common OIDs to monitor: interface status, bandwidth utilization, CPU load, memory usage, and error counters. Always use SNMP v3 in production — v1/v2c sends community strings in plaintext.
A user accidentally deleted important emails from their mailbox. How do you recover them?

Email recovery depends on how long ago and what email platform. In Microsoft 365/Exchange: First, check the Deleted Items folder — items are there until manually emptied or the retention period expires (default 30 days). If emptied from Deleted Items, check Recoverable Items: in Outlook, go to Deleted Items folder → Recover items recently removed from this folder (Home tab). Or in Outlook on the web: Deleted Items → Recover items deleted from this folder. This searches the 'Recoverable Items' dumpster, which retains items for 14 days by default (configurable up to 30 days). Admin recovery: if past the user's recovery window, admins can use eDiscovery (Compliance Center → Content Search) to search for and export the emails. For Exchange on-premises, restore from backup — mount the backup database as a recovery database and merge specific mailboxes. In Gmail: check Trash (items stay 30 days). For Google Workspace, admins can use Admin Console → Directory → select user → Restore Data to recover emails deleted within the last 25 days. If using Vault (Google's archiving), you can search and export archived emails regardless of deletion. Prevention: implement retention policies (M365 Compliance Center → Retention Policies) to prevent permanent deletion of emails matching certain criteria, and ensure regular mailbox backups with a third-party solution like Veeam or Barracuda.
Explain the concept of containers vs virtual machines.

Containers and VMs both provide isolation but at different levels. Virtual machines include a full operating system, virtual hardware, and a hypervisor layer. Each VM runs its own complete OS (kernel, drivers, system services) on top of virtualized hardware managed by a hypervisor (Type 1: ESXi, Hyper-V; Type 2: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation). VMs provide strong isolation since each has its own kernel, making them suitable for running different OS types and providing security boundaries. Overhead: GBs of memory and disk per VM, minutes to boot. Containers share the host OS kernel and isolate only the application and its dependencies using OS-level features (namespaces for isolation, cgroups for resource limits on Linux). A container image includes the application, libraries, and config — but not a full OS. Benefits: lightweight (MBs vs GBs), start in seconds, much higher density (hundreds of containers per host vs tens of VMs), consistent across dev/staging/prod environments. Container runtimes: Docker (most popular), containerd, CRI-O. Orchestration: Kubernetes (K8s) manages container deployment, scaling, and networking at scale. When to use VMs: different OS requirements, strong security isolation, legacy applications, licensed software that requires dedicated resources. When to use containers: microservices architecture, CI/CD pipelines, cloud-native applications, rapid scaling. Many organizations use both — containers running inside VMs for an extra layer of security.
How do you set up and configure a WSUS server for Windows updates?

WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) provides centralized Windows update management. Setup: 1) Install the WSUS role: Server Manager → Add Roles and Features → Windows Server Update Services. Choose database (WID for up to 20,000 clients, SQL Server for larger deployments). Select a local content storage path with adequate space (100GB+ recommended). 2) Post-installation: launch the WSUS Configuration Wizard. Choose to synchronize from Microsoft Update or an upstream WSUS server. Select products (Windows 10, Windows 11, Windows Server 2019/2022, Office, etc.) and classification types (Critical Updates, Security Updates, Definition Updates, Service Packs, Feature Updates). Set sync schedule (daily recommended, during off-hours). 3) Initial sync: start first synchronization — this downloads update metadata (not the actual files yet). Can take hours on first run. 4) Configure Automatic Approval Rules: WSUS Console → Options → Automatic Approvals. Create rules to auto-approve certain classifications (e.g., Definition Updates for Defender). 5) Create computer groups: WSUS Console → Computers → create groups (e.g., Pilot, Production-Servers, Production-Workstations). 6) Configure clients via GPO: Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → Windows Update. Set 'Specify intranet Microsoft update service location' to http://wsusserver:8530. Configure auto-update schedule, detection frequency, and target group. 7) Ongoing management: review and approve updates weekly, decline superseded updates, run the Server Cleanup Wizard monthly, monitor disk space, and check WSUS reports for compliance.
What are the common causes and fixes for the Windows Blue Screen of Death (BSOD)?

BSODs indicate a critical system error that Windows can't recover from. Common causes and fixes: 1) DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL / SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION — usually a faulty driver. Boot into Safe Mode (hold Shift while clicking Restart → Troubleshoot → Advanced → Startup Settings). Uninstall recently updated drivers, especially GPU, network, or USB drivers. Use 'Driver Verifier' (verifier.exe) to identify the problematic driver. 2) CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED — corrupted system files. Run 'sfc /scannow' from admin CMD, then 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth'. 3) MEMORY_MANAGEMENT / PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA — often bad RAM. Run Windows Memory Diagnostic (mdsched.exe) or the more thorough MemTest86 from a bootable USB. 4) KERNEL_DATA_INPAGE_ERROR / INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE — disk issues. Run 'chkdsk /r' on the system drive. Check SMART status. Replace failing drives. 5) WHEA_UNCORRECTABLE_ERROR — hardware failure, often CPU overheating or PSU issues. Check CPU temperatures, clean dust from heatsinks/fans, verify PSU output. 6) DPC_WATCHDOG_VIOLATION — typically storage controller driver issues, especially with SSDs. Update storage controller (AHCI/NVMe) drivers from manufacturer. Analysis: use WinDbg or BlueScreenView to analyze the minidump files (C:\Windows\Minidump\) — they identify the faulting module. If BSODs started after a Windows update, uninstall the recent update or use System Restore.
How do you set up a VPN server using WireGuard on Linux?

WireGuard is a modern, fast VPN protocol. Server setup on Ubuntu/Debian: 1) Install: 'sudo apt update && sudo apt install wireguard'. 2) Generate server keys: 'wg genkey | tee /etc/wireguard/server_private.key | wg pubkey > /etc/wireguard/server_public.key'. Set permissions: 'chmod 600 /etc/wireguard/server_private.key'. 3) Create server config (/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf): [Interface] section with Address = 10.0.0.1/24, ListenPort = 51820, PrivateKey = (contents of server_private.key). Add PostUp and PostDown rules for NAT: 'PostUp = iptables -A FORWARD -i wg0 -j ACCEPT; iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE' and corresponding PostDown to remove them. 4) Enable IP forwarding: 'echo net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 >> /etc/sysctl.conf && sysctl -p'. 5) Start WireGuard: 'sudo systemctl enable --now wg-quick@wg0'. 6) Generate client keys: 'wg genkey | tee client_private.key | wg pubkey > client_public.key'. 7) Add client peer to server config: [Peer] with PublicKey = (client public key), AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.2/32. 8) Create client config: [Interface] with PrivateKey, Address = 10.0.0.2/24, DNS = 1.1.1.1. [Peer] with server's PublicKey, Endpoint = server-public-ip:51820, AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0 (for full tunnel) or specific subnets (split tunnel), PersistentKeepalive = 25. 9) Open firewall port: 'sudo ufw allow 51820/udp'. Share client config via QR code ('qrencode -t ansiutf8 < client.conf') for mobile devices.
What is the principle of least privilege and how do you implement it in an IT environment?

The principle of least privilege (PoLP) states that users, applications, and systems should have only the minimum permissions necessary to perform their specific tasks — nothing more. Implementation across IT: Active Directory: Don't add users to Domain Admins for routine tasks. Create role-based security groups (e.g., Helpdesk-PasswordReset, Server-RDP-Access) with specific delegated permissions. Use fine-grained password policies. Implement a tiered administration model: Tier 0 (DC admins), Tier 1 (server admins), Tier 2 (workstation admins) — never use Tier 0 credentials on lower tiers. Endpoints: Remove local admin rights from standard users. Use tools like LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) for unique local admin passwords. Implement application whitelisting (AppLocker, Windows Defender Application Control). Cloud: Use IAM roles with specific policies instead of broad admin access. Implement just-in-time (JIT) access with Azure PIM (Privileged Identity Management) or AWS IAM Access Analyzer. Never use root/global admin accounts for daily tasks. Applications: Service accounts should run with minimal permissions. Database users should have access only to required tables/views. API keys should be scoped to needed endpoints. Network: Segment networks so users only access their segment. Use firewall rules defaulting to deny-all with explicit allows. Monitoring: implement privileged access monitoring (PAM) to log all admin actions, and regularly review access with access certifications.
How do you migrate an on-premises file server to SharePoint Online or OneDrive?

File server migration to SharePoint Online/OneDrive involves planning, assessment, and execution. Planning phase: audit your current file server — total size, number of files, folder structure, permissions, file types. SharePoint Online has limits: 400GB per file, 30 million items per library, 400 characters max path length. Identify files to exclude: PST files, executables, temporary files, duplicates, very old files that can be archived. Map existing folder structure to SharePoint sites and libraries — consider reorganizing around teams/projects rather than mirroring the drive letter structure. Map NTFS permissions to SharePoint/M365 groups. Migration tools: Microsoft SharePoint Migration Tool (SPMT) — free, handles files and permissions, supports scheduled migrations. Use Migration Manager in the SharePoint Admin Center for large-scale migrations with multiple agents. Third-party tools (ShareGate, AvePoint) offer more features like pre-migration reports, delta sync, and permission mapping. Execution: run a pilot migration with a small department first. Migrate during off-hours to minimize impact. Use delta sync for large shares — initial bulk copy, then incremental sync to catch changes. After migration: update GPO drive mappings to redirect to SharePoint, or deploy OneDrive with Known Folder Move. Train users on the new interface. Keep the file server read-only for a transition period, then decommission. Set up retention and sensitivity labels for governance.
A user reports their computer keeps restarting randomly. What do you check?

Random restarts indicate hardware issues, driver problems, or overheating. Systematic diagnosis: 1) Check Event Viewer first: Windows Logs → System, look for critical errors and 'Kernel-Power' Event ID 41 (unexpected shutdown). BugCheck entries reveal BSOD codes that triggered the restart (Windows auto-restarts on BSOD by default). 2) Disable automatic restart on failure to see the actual BSOD: right-click This PC → Properties → Advanced system settings → Startup and Recovery → uncheck 'Automatically restart'. 3) Temperature: install HWiNFO64 or Core Temp — CPU should stay below 85°C under load. If overheating, clean dust from fans/heatsinks, reapply thermal paste, ensure proper airflow. 4) Power supply: a failing PSU causes random shutdowns under load. Listen for unusual sounds, check if restarts happen during heavy use (gaming, rendering). Test with a known-good PSU or PSU tester. Check that all power cables are firmly seated. 5) RAM: run Windows Memory Diagnostic or MemTest86. Reseat RAM modules, try one stick at a time to identify faulty modules. 6) Drivers: update chipset, GPU, and network drivers. Check Device Manager for yellow triangles. 7) Disk health: check SMART status for failing drive warnings. 8) Windows Update: ensure OS is current, especially cumulative and driver updates. 9) Malware: run a full scan with Malwarebytes and Windows Defender. 10) If it only happens on battery (laptop), the battery may be failing — check battery health with 'powercfg /batteryreport'.
What is a DMZ in networking and how do you set one up?

A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is a network segment that sits between the external internet and the internal network, hosting public-facing services while protecting the internal network. Architecture options: Single firewall (three-legged): one firewall with three interfaces — external (internet), DMZ, and internal. The firewall controls traffic between all three zones. Simpler but a single point of failure. Dual firewall: an external firewall between internet and DMZ, and an internal firewall between DMZ and LAN. More secure because compromising one firewall doesn't expose the internal network. Use different vendors for defense in depth. Common DMZ services: web servers, email gateways (MX relay), DNS servers (public-facing), reverse proxies, VPN concentrators, FTP servers. Firewall rules: Internet → DMZ: allow only specific ports (80/443 for web, 25 for SMTP, 53 for DNS). DMZ → Internal: strictly limited — only specific connections needed (e.g., DMZ web server to internal database on port 1433 only). Internal → DMZ: allow management traffic (SSH, RDP from admin VLAN only). DMZ → Internet: limit to necessary outbound connections. Internal → Internet: through a proxy or NAT. Key principle: never allow direct traffic from internet to internal network. If a DMZ server is compromised, the internal firewall prevents lateral movement. Additional hardening: DMZ servers should be individually firewalled (host-based), run minimal services, be regularly patched, have IDS/IPS monitoring, and log all traffic to a SIEM on the internal network.
How do you troubleshoot Active Directory replication issues?

AD replication problems can cause login failures, stale group memberships, and GPO inconsistencies. Diagnosis: 1) Run 'repadmin /replsummary' — gives a quick overview of replication health across all DCs. Look for failures or high delta counts. 2) 'repadmin /showrepl' — shows detailed replication status for each naming context on a specific DC, including last replication time and any errors. 3) 'dcdiag /v' — comprehensive DC health check including replication, DNS, SYSVOL, time sync, and more. 4) Check Event Viewer: Directory Service log, DFS Replication log, DNS Server log. Common issues and fixes: DNS problems (most common cause): ensure all DCs point to another DC for DNS (never external DNS as primary). Run 'dcdiag /test:dns' to verify DNS health. Check _msdcs SRV records exist. Time synchronization: AD replication fails if time difference exceeds 5 minutes between DCs. The PDC emulator should sync to an external NTP source, and other DCs sync to it. Fix with 'w32tm /query /status' and 'w32tm /resync'. Network connectivity: verify DCs can reach each other on required ports (RPC: 135, LDAP: 389, SMB: 445, Kerberos: 88, DNS: 53). Lingering objects: 'repadmin /removelingeringobjects' cleans stale objects. SYSVOL replication: if using FRS, migrate to DFS-R. For DFS-R issues, check DFS Replication event log. Forcing replication: 'repadmin /syncall /AeD' forces replication across all DCs.
What is a service mesh and when would you use one?

A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication in a microservices architecture. Instead of each microservice implementing its own networking logic (retries, timeouts, encryption, load balancing), the service mesh provides these features transparently through sidecar proxies deployed alongside each service. How it works: a sidecar proxy (typically Envoy) is injected alongside each service pod in Kubernetes. All traffic in and out of the service goes through this proxy. A control plane (like Istio's istiod) configures all the proxies centrally. Key capabilities: Traffic management — canary deployments (route 5% of traffic to new version), A/B testing, circuit breaking (stop sending traffic to failing services), retries with backoff, rate limiting. Security — mutual TLS (mTLS) between all services automatically, fine-grained access policies (service A can call service B but not service C). Observability — distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin integration), metrics (latency, error rates, request volumes), service dependency graphs. Popular service meshes: Istio (most feature-rich, Kubernetes-native), Linkerd (lightweight, easier to operate), Consul Connect (HashiCorp, multi-platform). When to use: when you have many microservices (20+) that need consistent security, observability, and traffic policies. Don't use for monoliths or small service counts — the complexity overhead isn't justified.
How do you handle a situation where a user forgot their password and is locked out of their account?

Password reset and account unlock are among the most common IT support tasks. For Active Directory accounts: 1) Verify the user's identity — follow your organization's verification procedure (employee ID, manager confirmation, security questions, or video call). Never reset a password based solely on an email or phone call without verification. 2) Unlock the account: open AD Users and Computers → find the user → Properties → Account tab → check 'Unlock account'. PowerShell: 'Unlock-ADAccount -Identity username'. 3) Reset the password: right-click the user → Reset Password. Set a temporary password and check 'User must change password at next logon'. PowerShell: 'Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity username -Reset -NewPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString "TempPass123!" -AsPlainText -Force); Set-ADUser -Identity username -ChangePasswordAtLogon $true'. 4) Communicate the temporary password securely — never via email. Use a phone call, in-person, or a secure password delivery system. For Microsoft 365 cloud-only accounts: M365 Admin Center → Users → Active users → select user → Reset password. Or encourage self-service password reset (SSPR) if configured — users can reset via aka.ms/sspr using registered MFA methods. For reducing password reset tickets: implement Self-Service Password Reset (Azure AD SSPR), deploy password managers, consider passwordless authentication (Windows Hello, FIDO2 keys), and use SSO to reduce the number of passwords users need.
Explain the concept of high availability (HA) and common HA architectures.

High availability (HA) means designing systems to minimize downtime, typically targeting 99.9% uptime (8.76 hours/year downtime) or higher — 99.99% is 52 minutes/year, 99.999% (five nines) is 5.26 minutes/year. HA is achieved by eliminating single points of failure. Common HA architectures: Active-Passive (failover): a primary server handles all traffic while a standby server monitors it. If the primary fails, the standby takes over (failover). Examples: Windows Server Failover Clustering (WSFC), VMware HA, database mirroring. Simple but the standby server sits idle. Active-Active: multiple servers handle traffic simultaneously, with a load balancer distributing requests. If one server fails, others absorb its load. More efficient resource use. Examples: web server farms behind HAProxy/Nginx, SQL Always On Availability Groups with readable secondaries. N+1 redundancy: run one more server than needed — if any single server fails, the remaining servers can handle full load. Network HA: redundant switches with spanning tree or stacking, dual ISP connections with BGP failover, NIC teaming on servers, redundant firewalls in HA pairs. Storage HA: RAID for disk redundancy, SAN replication, distributed storage (Ceph, GlusterFS). Key components: health monitoring (heartbeat checks between nodes), automatic failover (no manual intervention needed), shared storage or data replication, virtual IP addresses (VIP) that float between nodes, and comprehensive testing — regularly test failover scenarios to ensure they actually work when needed.
How do you secure a newly deployed Windows Server?

Securing a new Windows Server follows a hardening checklist: 1) Updates: install all Windows Updates immediately. Enable automatic updates or configure WSUS. 2) Accounts: rename the default Administrator account. Set a strong password (20+ characters). Create individual admin accounts — never share the built-in admin. Disable the Guest account. 3) Remote access: enable RDP only if needed, restrict to specific IPs or VPN. Enable Network Level Authentication (NLA). Change the default RDP port (optional, security through obscurity). 4) Firewall: Windows Firewall should be ON for all profiles. Create explicit inbound rules only for required services. Block all inbound by default. 5) Services: disable unnecessary services (Print Spooler if not a print server, Windows Search on servers, Xbox services, etc.). Audit running services with 'Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq "Running"}'. 6) Roles: install only the roles and features needed — minimal attack surface. 7) Security policies: configure via Local Security Policy or GPO — account lockout (5 failed attempts, 30-minute lockout), password complexity, audit policies (log logon events, privilege use, object access). 8) Antivirus: ensure Windows Defender or enterprise AV is running with real-time protection and regular definition updates. 9) Logging: enable advanced audit policies, forward logs to a SIEM. 10) TLS: disable old protocols (SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, 1.1) via registry or IIS Crypto tool. 11) LAPS: deploy for local admin password management. 12) Backups: configure Windows Server Backup or enterprise backup solution. Test restores regularly.
What is SD-WAN and how does it differ from traditional WAN?

SD-WAN (Software-Defined Wide Area Network) is an approach to managing WAN connectivity that separates the networking hardware from its control mechanism, using software to intelligently direct traffic across multiple connection types. Traditional WAN typically relies on expensive MPLS circuits providing reliable, low-latency connections between sites, with static routing and manual configuration. SD-WAN advantages over traditional WAN: Cost savings — supplements or replaces expensive MPLS with cheaper broadband, LTE/5G, and direct internet access (DIA). You might keep one MPLS link for critical traffic and add two broadband links for other traffic. Application-aware routing — SD-WAN identifies applications and routes them based on policies. For example, route VoIP over the lowest-latency link, backups over the cheapest link, and critical ERP traffic over MPLS. Centralized management — configure and monitor all sites from a single cloud console (Cisco vManage, VMware VeloCloud Orchestrator, Fortinet FortiManager). Deploy new sites in hours instead of weeks. Direct cloud access — SD-WAN can route cloud-destined traffic (M365, Salesforce, AWS) directly to the internet from the branch, avoiding the latency of backhauling through headquarters. Built-in security — many SD-WAN solutions include firewall, IPS, URL filtering, and CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) — sometimes called SASE (Secure Access Service Edge). Automatic failover — if one link goes down, traffic automatically reroutes to available links within seconds, providing better reliability than a single MPLS circuit. Leading SD-WAN vendors: Cisco (Viptela/Meraki), VMware VeloCloud, Fortinet, Palo Alto Prisma SD-WAN, HPE Aruba.
How do you troubleshoot email delivery failures (bounced emails)?

Email bounces are classified as hard bounces (permanent) or soft bounces (temporary). Diagnosing: check the Non-Delivery Report (NDR) / bounce message — it contains SMTP error codes and diagnostic text. Common SMTP codes: 550 5.1.1 — recipient address doesn't exist. Verify the email address spelling. 550 5.7.1 — relaying denied or message rejected by policy. The recipient's server is blocking your mail. Check if your domain/IP is blacklisted at mxtoolbox.com/blacklists. 553 5.1.3 — malformed address syntax. 421 4.7.0 — temporary rate limiting. Your server is sending too much mail too fast. 550 5.7.25 / 550 5.7.26 — SPF/DKIM/DMARC authentication failure. Verify your DNS records: check SPF with 'nslookup -type=txt yourdomain.com', ensure the sending server's IP is included. Verify DKIM selector records exist. Check DMARC policy with 'nslookup -type=txt _dmarc.yourdomain.com'. 452 4.3.1 — insufficient system storage on recipient's server (temporary). 550 5.2.1 — recipient mailbox full. Troubleshooting steps: 1) Read the full NDR for specific error codes. 2) Test mail flow with telnet: 'telnet recipientmx.com 25' and walk through EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO manually. 3) Check your mail server logs (Exchange: Message Tracking, M365: Message Trace in Exchange Admin Center). 4) Verify MX records: 'nslookup -type=mx recipientdomain.com'. 5) Test email authentication: use mail-tester.com or mxtoolbox.com. 6) If blacklisted, request delisting and investigate why you were listed (compromised account sending spam, open relay, etc.).
What is Kubernetes and what problem does it solve?

Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform originally developed by Google. It automates deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications. Problems it solves: Without Kubernetes, managing containers at scale requires manually handling deployment across servers, restarting failed containers, scaling up during traffic spikes, load balancing, service discovery, rolling updates without downtime, and managing configuration and secrets — all of which becomes unmanageable beyond a few containers. Core concepts: Pod — the smallest deployable unit, contains one or more containers that share networking and storage. Deployment — manages replicas of pods, handles rolling updates and rollbacks. Service — provides stable networking (a permanent IP/DNS name) for a set of pods, with built-in load balancing. Namespace — logical isolation within a cluster (dev, staging, prod). Ingress — manages external HTTP/HTTPS access to services, handles SSL termination and routing rules. ConfigMap/Secret — externalize configuration and sensitive data from container images. PersistentVolume — provides persistent storage that survives pod restarts. Key features: self-healing (restarts failed containers, replaces unhealthy pods), horizontal auto-scaling (scales pods based on CPU/memory/custom metrics), rolling updates (zero-downtime deployments), service discovery (DNS-based or environment variables), and declarative configuration (define desired state in YAML, K8s makes it so). Managed Kubernetes offerings: AWS EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE — these handle the control plane so you only manage worker nodes and workloads.
How do you set up centralized logging for a multi-server environment?

Centralized logging aggregates logs from all servers, applications, and network devices into a single platform for searching, analysis, and alerting. Popular stacks: ELK/Elastic Stack: Elasticsearch (storage and search engine), Logstash (log processing and parsing), Kibana (visualization and dashboards). Add Filebeat on each server as a lightweight log shipper. Setup: install Filebeat on each server, configure it to read log files (syslog, application logs, IIS/Apache logs) and forward to Logstash or directly to Elasticsearch. Logstash applies parsing rules (grok patterns to extract fields like timestamp, severity, source IP). Elasticsearch indexes the parsed logs. Kibana provides search, dashboards, and alerting. Alternative: Grafana Loki — lighter weight, uses labels instead of full-text indexing, cheaper to run. Pair with Promtail for log collection and Grafana for visualization. For Windows environments: configure Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) to centralize Windows event logs to a collector server, then ship to your logging platform. Or use Winlogbeat to ship Windows events directly to Elasticsearch. For cloud: AWS CloudWatch Logs, Azure Monitor Logs, Google Cloud Logging provide managed solutions. Key practices: standardize log formats across applications (JSON is ideal), include correlation IDs for tracing requests across services, set retention policies (hot/warm/cold storage tiers), create alerts for critical errors, build dashboards for each application team, and secure log transport with TLS encryption.
What steps do you take when onboarding a new employee from an IT perspective?

IT onboarding ensures new employees are productive from day one. Pre-arrival (1-2 weeks before): receive new hire request from HR with start date, department, role, and manager. Create Active Directory account with appropriate OU, groups, and permissions based on role template. Create M365/email account and assign licenses. Provision hardware — laptop/desktop per department standards, configure with company image (OS, standard software, security tools, VPN client). Create accounts in business applications (CRM, ERP, ticketing system, etc.) as specified by the role template. Set up phone/extension if needed. Prepare welcome documentation (IT handbook, acceptable use policy, password policy). Day one: meet the new employee, provide hardware and peripherals. Walk through initial login process — domain login, password change, MFA enrollment (authenticator app setup). Verify email access (Outlook, Teams). Connect to Wi-Fi, VPN setup and testing. Verify access to shared drives/SharePoint sites, printers, and business applications. Review IT policies — acceptable use, security awareness, how to contact support. First week follow-up: verify all systems are working, address any access issues, ensure they've completed security awareness training. Automation: use PowerShell scripts or identity management tools (SailPoint, Okta) to automate account creation from HR system data. Implement role-based access templates so permissions are consistent. Document the onboarding checklist in your ticketing system as a template for repeatability. Include offboarding dates for contractors/temporary employees from the start.
